name: 2 Corinthians
author: The letter comes from Paul, a Jewish man from Tarsus who had been a Pharisee, a strict teacher of Jewish law, before becoming a follower of Jesus. He worked as a travelling apostle, a missionary who started churches across the Roman world, and supported himself by making tents. He had founded the church in Corinth himself around AD 50–51. Nearly everyone accepts Paul wrote it, though many scholars think the book joins two or more of his letters to Corinth, while others read it as one letter.
audience: It was written to the church in Corinth, mostly non-Jewish converts with some Jewish believers, and to Christians across Achaia, the Roman province of southern Greece. Paul's relationship with them had become strained, with a painful visit, a sorrowful letter, and visiting rival teachers who questioned his authority.
era: Paul probably wrote around AD 55–56 from Macedonia in northern Greece, during the early reign of the emperor Nero. Corinth was a wealthy, busy Roman colony and trading port, rebuilt by Julius Caesar a century earlier, full of temples, merchants and travelling speakers. Paul was also gathering money from his non-Jewish churches to help poor believers in Jerusalem.

notes.1:1: Paul names Timothy, his younger co-worker, as co-sender, and addresses believers throughout Achaia as well as the church in Corinth.
notes.1:3: Paul had recently faced deadly danger in the province of Asia, in today's western Turkey; the exact event is unknown, though some link it to trouble in Ephesus.
notes.1:15: Paul had changed his announced travel plans to visit Corinth, and some there accused him of being unreliable.
notes.1:23: After a painful visit, Paul sent a sorrowful letter instead of coming again; it is probably lost, though some think chapters 10–13 preserve it.
notes.2:5: One church member had caused Paul and the church serious hurt and had been disciplined by the congregation; who he was is not known.
notes.2:12: Troas was a port in northwest Asia Minor; Paul waited there for Titus to bring news from Corinth, then crossed to Macedonia.
notes.2:14: Rival teachers had arrived in Corinth carrying letters of recommendation, a common way travellers proved they could be trusted.
notes.3:7: This section recalls Moses' face shining after he received the law on Mount Sinai, when he covered it with a veil.
notes.4:7: Clay jars were cheap, everyday pottery, commonly used in the ancient world for storing goods and even valuables.
notes.6:14: Corinth was full of temples to Greek and Roman gods; some scholars think this section came from another letter because it seems to interrupt the surrounding flow.
notes.7:2: Titus finally met Paul in Macedonia, bringing news of how the Corinthians had received his sorrowful letter.
notes.8:1: The Macedonian churches, such as those at Philippi and Thessalonica, were themselves poor and under pressure, yet had given generously to the Jerusalem collection.
notes.8:16: Paul sent Titus with two unnamed fellow believers, one chosen by the churches, to oversee the collection openly and honestly.
notes.9:1: Paul had told the Macedonians that the believers of Achaia had been preparing their gift since the previous year.
notes.10:1: Critics in Corinth said Paul was forceful in letters but unimpressive in person; the sharper tone here leads many to see chapters 10–13 as a separate letter.
notes.11:1: Paul answers visiting teachers he calls super-apostles, impressive speakers who boasted of their credentials and probably had Jewish backgrounds.
notes.11:7: Paul refused payment from the Corinthians, working instead and accepting help from Macedonia, though in Greek culture respected teachers usually accepted patrons' support.
notes.11:16: Paul's escape from Damascus in a basket happened in the late 30s AD, when the city was under an official of King Aretas IV of Nabatea.
notes.12:1: Paul describes a vision from fourteen years earlier, around the early 40s AD, and an ongoing affliction whose exact nature has never been known.
notes.12:14: Paul was preparing for his third visit to Corinth, after his founding stay and the later painful visit.

flags.problem: The letters of recommendation come up at 3:1, not 2:14. Verse 2:14 uses the picture of a Roman victory parade, so a reader at 2:14 gets a note about something the verse does not mention.
flags.suggestion: Move the letters-of-recommendation note to 3:1. For 2:14, explain the Roman triumph: a victorious general's parade through the city, with captives and burning incense.

flags.problem: The deadly danger in Asia is described from 1:8. Verses 1:3–7 speak of comfort in suffering in general, so the note does not match what the reader is looking at.
Titus reaching Paul in Macedonia is told from 7:5. Verses 7:2–4 are Paul's appeal for the Corinthians' affection, so the note sits a few verses early.
